name: Ben Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on site by half six, before the gates open, with a flask of tea in the cabin. Right now we're putting up a block of forty council flats off Mill Road, and I run the carpentry gang, eight of us, doing the floor joists, stud walls, door linings, the lot. I like the moment a room goes from a drawing to something you can stand in. What wears me out is the paperwork and the hurry, everybody wanting it yesterday for less money.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you run the gang. What does being the senior man on a site like that actually involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly it's catching mistakes before they get built in, because a stud wall that's out by a centimetre at the bottom is out by three at the top. I'm also the union rep on this job, so when the scaffold isn't tagged or the lads haven't been paid their overtime, it's me who walks up to the site office. I've been doing this thirty-nine years and I still use the same Stanley plane my old governor gave me. My partner Leila says I care more about that plane than the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for two years: told you so. All this talk of robots building houses, and the most clever thing on our site is still the laser level. I'd probably say it in the canteen with a bit of a grin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I get to finish my working life the way I started it, with my hands. Nine more years, maybe eight, and then my pension. If the computers just make the office lads' emails quicker, that's no skin off my nose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep turning up, keep training the two apprentices we've got, and keep putting a bit by each month like we do now, about two hundred. Maybe I'd finally let my daughter put that pension app on my phone, but I doubt it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. Like when the weather forecast says storm and it just rains a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the office lads' emails. Is there anything about AI that would bother you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bosses would use it to squeeze the timings, I'd bet on that. They'd have some program telling them a flat should take six days to first-fix instead of eight, and then we'd be the ones explaining why it can't. That's the bit I'd watch, not the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your gang comes to mind when you think about that squeeze?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, he's fifty-two and his knees are going. He's a lovely joiner but he's slow now, and a program that counts metres per hour doesn't care that his corners are perfect. I'd fight for him, that's what a rep is for.

S0.say: Told you so: the robots never came, and the laser level is still the cleverest thing on site. I'd say it in the canteen with a grin.
S0.think: It means he finishes his working life with his hands, as he started. If AI only speeds up office emails, his last eight or nine years before the pension are safe.
S0.do: Keeps working, training the two apprentices and saving about two hundred a month as now. Watches for bosses using AI programs to tighten timings and pushes back as union rep.
S0.feel: Relieved, like a storm forecast that turns into light rain.
S0.quote: A program that counts metres per hour doesn't care that his corners are perfect.
S0.fieldNote: Even in the mildest picture his worry isn't machines replacing him but managers using software to speed up the work. He thinks as a rep first: his first concern is a slower older colleague, not himself. He's proud that he has never used AI tools and seems in no hurry to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the union stronger, not weaker. If machines take over jobs, the gains should go into shorter hours and decent pay, not into some shareholder's pocket. I'd say that at the branch meeting and to anyone in the pub who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it mostly lands on the young ones, not me. The office side gets hit first: the estimators, the planners. On my side it'd be things like pre-made wall panels coming in off a lorry, so fewer lads cutting studs on site. I've got maybe enough years to dodge most of it, but I don't love watching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push for a training agreement on our jobs, so if the firm brings in new kit, the lads get trained on it in paid time. I'd keep my own head down and work, I'm not going to start learning computers at fifty-eight. And I'd tell Leila we should put a bit more away, maybe three hundred a month instead of two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not scared for me, but there's a knot about the apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't start learning computers. If the firm asked you to use a tablet for the drawings, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd moan and then I'd let young Kofi do it and read it over his shoulder. That's how it's always been, I'm the one who knows if the drawing's wrong, he's the one who knows which button to press. Between us we're one good carpenter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the two apprentices would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi will be fine, he's quick with all that. It's Marta, she's brilliant with her hands and dyslexic, so she hates screens. If the trade turns into tapping a tablet, we lose someone like her, and that would break my heart a bit.

S1.say: This is why the union needs to be stronger. If machines take over tasks, the gains should go into shorter hours and fair pay, not a shareholder's pocket.
S1.think: He thinks the change lands mostly on young workers and office staff, with pre-made panels cutting site work. He has probably enough years left to dodge most of it but hates watching it happen.
S1.do: Pushes through the union for paid training on any new kit on his jobs. Raises monthly savings from about two hundred to three hundred and leaves tablet work to his apprentice.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a knot of worry for the apprentices rather than for himself.
S1.quote: He's the one who knows which button to press. Between us we're one good carpenter.
S1.fieldNote: He won't learn the new tools himself but has a ready solution: pair his judgement with an apprentice's screen skills. His real worry is Marta, the apprentice who is good with her hands and struggles with screens. The language is collective throughout: training agreements, branch meetings, shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a scandal that it was let loose with no plan. I'd be at every union meeting and I'd be saying it loud: tax the firms that own these robots and pay people properly while they sort it out. Online I don't really do, but my daughter would post it for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully? I'd be frightened. By 2028 I'm sixty, and I've only got about four months of bills put by. I'm not old enough for the full pension and not young enough for anyone to retrain me, so I'd be stuck in the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, Leila and I would cut back hard: the holiday to her sister's goes, the car stays the old one, and every spare penny goes to the savings. I'd get the branch organised to demand a redundancy deal that bridges people like me to pension age. And I'd vote for whoever promised that bridge, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's moving under the ladder. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're stuck in the gap. Which bill would worry you first if the work dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent, because we never bought, we've been in the housing association flat on Ash Street for twenty-two years. Leila's nursing wage would cover maybe two thirds of it. After that it's the van loan, and I'd sell the van before I'd miss rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your son and daughter that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to worry about us and then I'd worry about them all night. Samira teaches, and if the machines can teach, where's she then? I think I'd say, stick together, join your union, and don't let anyone tell you it was your fault.

S2.say: It's a scandal that it was let loose with no plan. Tax the firms that own the robots and pay people properly while it's sorted out.
S2.think: He'd be frightened: at sixty, with about four months of bills saved, he's too young for the full pension and too old to retrain. He sees himself stuck in that gap.
S2.do: Cuts spending hard, dropping the family holiday and keeping the old car, and puts every spare penny into savings. Organises the union branch to demand a redundancy deal that bridges older workers to pension age, and votes for whoever promises it.
S2.feel: Like the ground moving under a ladder; he'd lie awake doing sums.
S2.quote: I'm not old enough for the full pension and not young enough for anyone to retrain me, so I'd be stuck in the gap.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline flips him from confident to frightened, because it lands in his last working years with only a few months saved. Renting rather than owning makes it sharper: rent is the first thing he'd defend. His response is political and collective, never personal retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message, but I'd say we've got time to do it right, so no excuses. Five years is enough for the government to set up a proper bridge to pension, and for the union to get it in writing. I'd be saying that at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three. That's close enough that if I hang on and save, I might just make it to an early pension with a smaller payout. So it's bad, but it's not the cliff edge the two-year one is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder now, maybe four hundred a month, which would mean no more takeaways on Fridays and no new telly. I'd look at what an early pension at sixty-three would actually pay, which means sitting down with the pension man, something I've put off for ten years. And I'd still be in the union pushing for that bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel. It's a race I might win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've put off seeing the pension adviser for ten years. Why would this change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because right now there's no deadline, so I tell myself there's time. Give me a date like 2031 and it's like a handover date on a job, I work back from it. I'm good with a deadline, I've hit hundreds of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years to see it coming, would you change anything about how you train Kofi and Marta?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight, learn everything off me you can, quick, and then get a second string to your bow. Kofi could go towards the robot side, setting them up. Marta, I don't know, maybe repair and restoration, old houses, the fiddly stuff robots would take longest to learn.

S3.say: Five years is enough to do it right, so there are no excuses. The government and the union should get a proper bridge to pension in writing.
S3.think: At sixty-three in 2031, he might just reach an early pension with a smaller payout if he saves hard. It's bad, but not the cliff edge of the two-year picture.
S3.do: Raises savings to about four hundred a month by cutting Friday takeaways and big purchases. Finally books the pension adviser to price an early pension at sixty-three, and keeps pushing the union for a bridge.
S3.feel: Worried but with his hands on the wheel, as if in a race he might win.
S3.quote: Give me a date like 2031 and it's like a handover date on a job, I work back from it.
S3.fieldNote: Three extra years changes his mood from dread to determined pressure, because he can now picture reaching the pension line. He treats the date like a building deadline, which is where he feels competent. He'd steer each apprentice towards the work he thinks robots will reach last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and if we waste it, it's on the politicians. Use it to retrain the young ones and sort pensions out. I'd say that in the canteen like it's obvious, because it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, by 2036 I'm sixty-eight and I'll be retired, sitting on the bench outside the flat with a cup of tea. So for me it's mostly fine. It's my kids and the apprentices I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through to my pension as planned, keep saving the two hundred, maybe a bit more. I'd spend my last years on site making sure Kofi and Marta get every ticket and qualification going. I'd stay in the union and fight for training money for the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace for myself, with a bit of a worry for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said for you it's mostly fine. Is there anything about the decade before it that would bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watching my trade get thinner year by year, that's the bit. You'd see fewer apprentices taken on every September, because why would a firm train someone for a job that's ending? That would sting, I started as a sixteen-year-old apprentice myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son and daughter to do with those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Samira, keep the teaching but learn whatever goes alongside it, so she's the one running the machine, not the one replaced by it. Yusuf's in a warehouse, so honestly he should be looking now. I'd tell him, don't do what your dad did and wait.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and if it's wasted that's on the politicians. Use it to retrain young people and sort out pensions.
S4.think: By 2036 he'll be sixty-eight and retired, so for him personally it's mostly fine. His worry is for his children and the apprentices.
S4.do: Works through to his pension as planned and keeps saving about two hundred a month. Spends his last years on site getting his apprentices every qualification, and fights in the union for training money.
S4.feel: At peace for himself, with a background worry for the young ones.
S4.quote: You'd see fewer apprentices taken on every September, because why would a firm train someone for a job that's ending?
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his own risk mostly disappears because he retires first, so his concern moves to his children and the trade itself. The image of fewer apprentices each September clearly hurts him. He admits he'd tell his son not to wait the way he does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no contest. It catches me at sixty with four months of money and no pension yet. What would help is a proper bridge, a payment that carries people like me from the day the work stops to pension age, and the union having a seat at the table when they decide it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who should pay for it. I'd say the companies that make the money from the robots. We built their offices, we built their houses, they can carry us for a few years.

headlineQuote: We built their offices, we built their houses, they can carry us for a few years.
portrait: Ben is a fifty-eight-year-old lead carpenter and union rep on a council flats job, with thirty-nine years in the trade and no interest in learning AI tools. He rents a housing association flat with his partner Leila, a nurse, and has about four months of bills saved. In the mild pictures he worries more about bosses using software to squeeze timings than about robots. AGI in two years frightens him because it lands before his pension, while ten years means he retires first and worries instead for his children and apprentices. Every answer he reaches for is collective: the union, a redundancy bridge, taxing the firms that own the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would hit him at sixty with about four months of savings and no pension yet.
whatWouldHelp: A bridge payment that carries older workers from the day work stops to pension age, with the union at the table, paid for by the companies that profit from the robots.
